questions.question: Under a Poisson change model with rate lambda, what is the probability of at least one change by time t?
options: 1 minus exp(-lambda times t)
lambda divided by t
exp(lambda plus t)
1 divided by lambda times t

questions.question: What should count as a meaningful page change?
options: Any byte difference, including a timestamp that rotates on every request
A semantic content difference measured after normalized extraction
A change in the compression or caching headers the server returned
A change to the URL path that the canonicalizer failed to collapse

questions.question: A page changes three times over 30 observed days. What is the simple raw rate estimate?
options: 0.01 per day
0.03 per day
0.10 per day
10 per day

questions.question: Why use a prior for a newly discovered page?
options: One unchanged fetch already pins the page's long-run rate precisely
A prior forces every page class onto one shared estimated change rate value
A prior removes the need to keep fetch history and content hashes
Sparse observations should be smoothed with evidence from similar pages

questions.question: Why can weekly polling underestimate a fast page's change rate?
options: Several changes between polls are observed as one content difference
Each poll recovers every intermediate version the publisher has produced
A Poisson model forbids a page from changing more than once ever
A changed content hash is recorded as zero observed intervals

questions.question: Why keep both raw and semantic content hashes?
options: They certify that the semantic extractor contains no parser defects
They separate transport and template churn from real content change
They remove the need to store or calibrate HTTP validators at all
They make every publisher-supplied timestamp trustworthy by construction

questions.question: What does age since last successful verification do to change probability?
options: It drives the probability toward zero the longer the page sits unverified
It plays no part in any expected-value scheduling model
It raises the accumulated probability that a change has occurred
It converts expected fetch cost into a document-frequency weight

questions.question: Why divide expected stale-content benefit by fetch cost?
options: To favour the largest files, since they carry the most text per fetch made
To give every URL in the frontier an identical revisit frequency
To let cost replace importance and change rate in the priority score
To spend limited capacity where each unit of resource buys most value

questions.question: Page A has higher importance and change rate than older Page B at equal cost. Why can A rank first?
options: Expected value combines importance and change probability, not age alone
The older page must always be fetched first once its age exceeds a week
Change rate drops out of the score whenever two pages share a fetch cost
Importance applies only at ranking time, after the document is served

questions.question: Why use a two-level host and URL scheduler?
options: So one high-rate host can take every worker while its queue is deep
So host eligibility is enforced before the best URL on it is chosen
So robots rules and provider backoff can be skipped during a recrawl
So every host collapses to a single canonical URL in the frontier

questions.question: Why impose a maximum audit interval on apparently static pages?
options: So static pages are fetched continuously regardless of estimated rate
So low-rate pages can be dropped from scope once the estimate settles
So an uncertain low estimate cannot starve a page of revalidation
So every unchanged response is escalated as a probable server error

questions.question: A worker writes fetched content but loses its acknowledgment. How should a retry behave?
options: Write a second document version, since the first commit cannot be confirmed
Assume the earlier write failed and reset the page's change history
Delete every stored version of the URL before fetching the page again
Key the output on URL plus content hash so the same result is recognized

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: What does an exponential recency decay with half-life h mean?
options: The recency signal falls to half its value when the age reaches h
The relevance score drops to zero once the document is older than h
Documents older than h are removed from the index at the next merge
The query's recency weight doubles for every h days of document age

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: Why should recency not replace relevance?
options: Every information need is satisfied by whichever page was published last
Timeless and historical queries often prefer older authoritative material
Recency cannot be derived from any timestamp the corpus actually stores
A newer document is guaranteed to be relevant to whatever query found it first

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: With a 30-day half-life, what recency value does a 90-day-old document have relative to a new one?

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: Why is crawl time a poor default content-freshness date?
options: It predates publication by several years for most archived documents
It is not available to acquisition systems until indexing completes
It moves only when the page's semantic content has actually changed
A recently fetched old document would look artificially fresh

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: A query asks specifically about a 2024 policy. What should happen before generic newest-first boosting?
options: Filter or resolve the requested effective period with temporal understanding
Demote every 2024 document, since a newer revision is always the correct one
Treat crawl time as the validity date, since it is the only trusted stamp
Raise the recency weight to its maximum so the newest revision wins outright

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: Why evaluate recency by temporal query class?
options: One global average is enough to expose regressions on evergreen queries
A freshness boost helps mutable queries and can damage historical ones
Temporal intent never surfaces explicitly in the words users type
Every query class should share one recency weight for comparability
